🐾 Here’s the story Matt tells when asked about a time he failed.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on that documentation rather than verifying the controls. He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed, assumptions he should have verified rather than inherited.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Following the incident, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

On a global platform modernization for a financial services client, Matt failed to verify the controls protecting production customer data. He was the tech lead, responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup across development, QA, UAT, and production.

The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases. Matt relied on that documentation rather than confirming it was accurate. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, verify that customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that “leaders own the environment their teams operate in.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one responsibilities in his delivery approach, rather than assumptions inherited from earlier phases.
